evidence_records.Generated outputs: parent/child codebooks, saturation points, source excerpts with assigned codes and overarching themes
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: The study audits source-excerpt overlap and quote fidelity, including summaries and interviewer-only errors, but complete outputs and transcript mappings are not public.
evidence_records.Baselines: traditional human Dedoose analysis, out-of-the-box GPT-4o and knowledge-base/RAG GPT-4o
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one end-to-end analysis per LLM configuration is apparent; seeds, reruns and order randomization are not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: code/theme counts, saturation transcript count, excerpt-count and length distributions, exact/partial overlap, missed/unique excerpts, multi-code rates, labor hours and cost
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Direct human baseline with double-coding on 20 transcripts; conceptual code/theme mapping was conducted by the research team but not independently blinded.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: one lead qualitative expert, another code-development contributor, two human coders familiar with the schema, and one postdoctoral LLM operator; exact credentials for every comparison judgment are not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: Cohen's kappa = 0.84 between the two human coders on the 20-transcript subset; this is not human–LLM agreement
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive counts, ranges, means, percentages and overlap mappings; no uncertainty intervals or significance tests
evidence_records.Principal results: Humans produced 7 parent/65 child codes and 9 themes; both LLMs produced 10 parent/22 child codes and 6 themes. Both missed 190/428 human excerpts; out-of-the-box overlapped 238/428 (56%) and knowledge-base 124/428 (29%). Knowledge-base outputs included 68/251 (27%) interpretive summaries instead of quotes. Humans multi-coded more often (38% versus 23% and 8%) and one-third of human themes were absent from both LLMs.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: Human work was reported as about 110 hours, CAD $3,537 labor plus $74.24 Dedoose; LLM work required about 40 researcher hours, CAD $1,260 labor plus $12.10 API cost. Review labor remains substantial and the comparison excludes downstream correction costs.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: The source trial received ethical approval in April 2023 and is registered as NCT05923398. Transcripts were anonymized through an AI-assisted plus manual transcription workflow, and no PII was sent to the LLM.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Supplementary 1 contains RISEN prompts and Supplementary 2 cost details; code, model snapshot, complete outputs and restricted transcripts are not available
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: One GPT family, one health-care-professional corpus, limited patient generalizability, model/prompt dependence, privacy risk for future patient use, training-data bias, output variability and environmental cost
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The abstract grammatically links “strong inter-rater reliability (κ=.84)” to the out-of-the-box LLM, but κ=.84 is explicitly the human–human baseline. Faster apparent saturation reflects smaller, coarser codebooks and should not be interpreted as superior analytical completeness. Single runs leave stability unknown.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Uses qualitative data from the DHMI-S trial and compares against a pre-existing human analysis; not a duplicate of other LLM-thematic-analysis papers.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Strong evidence for quote-level recall/fidelity auditing, granularity and multi-code metrics, direct labor accounting and a human-first baseline. It materially argues against saturation speed or theme-count overlap as sufficient quality evidence.

evidence_records.Full citation: Nam, Hyunji, Lucia Langlois, James Malamut, Mei Tan, and Dorottya Demszky. 2025. IDEAlign: Comparing Large Language Models to Human Experts in Open-ended Interpretive Annotations. arXiv:2509.02855v1.
evidence_records.Title: IDEAlign: Comparing Large Language Models to Human Experts in Open-ended Interpretive Annotations
evidence_records.Authors: Hyunji Nam; Lucia Langlois; James Malamut; Mei Tan; Dorottya Demszky
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: not peer reviewed in the inspected version
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1 posted 2025-09-02; no archival version identified
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: IDEAlign open-ended interpretive-annotation evaluation framework
evidence_records.Research objective: Develop and validate a scalable expert benchmark for idea-level similarity among open-ended human and LLM annotations, and test lexical, embedding, topic-model and LLM-judge metrics against it.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: expert evaluation of open-ended interpretive annotations, presented as relevant to thematic analysis and educational feedback
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Experts choose the odd annotation in repeated triplets; aggregate co-selection yields pairwise similarity scores. Automated metrics rank the same pairs, and their Spearman correlations with expert rankings are evaluated on math-reasoning annotations and essay feedback. No codebook or theme generation is performed.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: neither; comparative evaluation of free-text interpretive outputs under task-specific criteria
evidence_records.Domain: education / classroom reasoning and writing feedback
evidence_records.Dataset name: four deidentified mathematics-classroom transcripts and 18 open-source student essays with expert and LLM annotations
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: GitHub shares full math annotations and consent-permitted feedback subsets; some feedback is restricted by original consent
evidence_records.Number of participants: 11 math annotation authors, 10 additional math similarity judges, 32 ELA feedback providers from prior work and 7 ELA similarity judges; source student counts are not fully reported here
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: math transcripts contain 300–600 lines each; 640 math triplet judgments and 458 feedback judgments; 18 essays
evidence_records.Document length: math annotations average 139.38 words, maximum 556; source transcript/essay token lengths otherwise not summarized
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: deidentified classroom data involving students, teachers and guardians; essay feedback shared only where consent permits
evidence_records.Model family: OpenAI GPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini and DeepSeek; 16 embedding models plus topic models
evidence_records.Exact model/version: annotation generators include ChatGPT, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 2.5 Pro and DeepSeek-V2.5; judges include GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini, Claude 4 Sonnet and Claude 3.5 Sonnet
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Binary, continuous and IDEAlign pick-the-odd-one-out prompts with explicit content-not-style criteria; full templates are provided in the appendix
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: no fine-tuning; PCA post-processing, BERTopic/UMAP/HDBSCAN and MALLET-LDA hyperparameter variants were evaluated
evidence_records.Agent roles: annotation generator in source datasets and similarity judge in the benchmark
evidence_records.Human role: Expert educators generated interpretive annotations, labeled triplets, defined domain-relevant similarity criteria and served as the gold ranking; authors designed aggregation and perturbation tests.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: triplet judgment and resulting annotation-pair similarity ranking
evidence_records.Generated outputs: expert pairwise similarity scores, automated similarity rankings, correlations, style-perturbation sensitivity and bootstrap sample-size guidance
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Every similarity judgment is tied to three annotations of the same source item; task IDs, annotations, metadata and expert mappings are shared to the extent consent allows.
evidence_records.Baselines: BLEU, 16 embedding models with/without PCA, BERTopic, MALLET-LDA, binary/continuous LLM judges and a bootstrapped human-evaluation oracle
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: 10 sampled responses per pairwise LLM-judge comparison; 100 bootstrap runs for sample-size/stability analysis; two LLM-generated annotations per model in the math source task
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Spearman rank correlation, bootstrap human-oracle correlation, percentage change under style perturbation and sample-size stability
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Domain experts labeled randomized triplets through a web interface using explicit idea-level criteria; math and ELA tasks had separate expert panels.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: 10 math educators for 640 triplets and 7 ELA teachers for 458 judgments; ELA judges had 5–6 or at least 8 years of teaching experience and were compensated $50/hour
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: No conventional kappa reported; bootstrapped human-evaluation oracle correlations were 0.906 for feedback and 0.812 for reasoning.
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: Spearman correlations, 100-run bootstrap curves and perturbation comparisons
evidence_records.Principal results: Best GPT-4.1 IDEAlign correlations were .618 (feedback) and .683 (reasoning), versus best vector results .489/.491 and human oracle .906/.812. Triplet prompting improved alignment 9–30%. Style-only edits inflated embedding similarities by up to 82%, versus +5% for GPT-4.1 and −2.03% for Sonnet 4. Stable rankings required roughly 300 feedback and 600 reasoning judgments.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: Expert labeling is explicitly recognized as costly; judges were paid $50/hour. No complete dollar comparison with automated metrics is reported.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Math classroom data were collected under IRB #75294 with teacher, student and guardian consent; judges saw only deidentified data and were compensated. Feedback sharing follows prior consent limitations.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: code, prompts, annotation data, metadata and task mappings: https://github.com/EduNLP/IDEAlign
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Only two educational tasks; similarity criteria must be defined with domain experts and can change by task; expert data are costly; LLM judges still lack domain expertise and broader-domain validation is needed
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The framework validates similarity-to-expert judgments, not the truth or qualitative adequacy of an annotation. Aggregating plurality into one scalar ranking can conceal substantively different expert perspectives, and the same experts do not judge every possible domain.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Builds on previously collected math-transcript annotations and essay-feedback data; this paper contributes the evaluation benchmark rather than a new thematic-analysis system.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: A high-value adjacent foundation for idea-level human evaluation, metric validation, perturbation testing and sample-size planning. It supports triplet expert judgments as an alternative to lexical similarity, while requiring separate source-grounding and plurality analyses.

evidence_records.Full citation: Castellanos, Arturo, Haoqiang Jiang, Paulo Gomes, Debra Vander Meer, and Alfred Castillo. 2025. Large Language Models for Thematic Summarization in Qualitative Health Care Research: Comparative Analysis of Model and Human Performance. JMIR AI 4:e64447. https://doi.org/10.2196/64447.
evidence_records.Title: Large Language Models for Thematic Summarization in Qualitative Health Care Research: Comparative Analysis of Model and Human Performance
evidence_records.Authors: Arturo Castellanos; Haoqiang Jiang; Paulo Gomes; Debra Vander Meer; Alfred Castillo
evidence_records.Publication history notes: published 2025-04-04; PubMed PMID 40611510 and open full text inspected
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; publisher/PMC full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: nurse-forum LDA analysis family; extends the authors' 2023 JMIR Nursing study DOI 10.2196/40676
evidence_records.Research objective: Test whether LLMs can scale the interpretation and labeling of LDA topics from a health-care forum and compare human and model themes.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive semantic thematic analysis/thematic summarization layered on topic modeling
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: LDA produced 310 topics from preprocessed nurse-forum posts. Two humans labeled each topic after reading its top 10 posts and derived 58 subthemes. GPT-3.5 generated themes/subthemes from the same topic samples; two authors placed human–LLM comparisons on a novel seven-category scale. GPT-4 then judged alignment, convergence, coherence and complementarity of the human and GPT-3.5 themes.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: claimed inductive; operationally constrained by LDA clusters, top-post selection and fixed comparison criteria
evidence_records.Domain: health-care / nurses' online discussion during COVID-19
evidence_records.Dataset name: public Nurse Forum posts aggregated over 28 two-week periods, March 2020–April 2021
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: source described as public and anonymized; analyzed corpus and mappings not deposited with the paper
evidence_records.Number of documents: number of forum posts not reported; 310 LDA topic clusters were analyzed through their top 10 posts
evidence_records.Number of participants: number and identity of forum contributors not reported
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 28 biweekly periods; 310 topics; up to 3,100 topic-post presentations before possible repeated posts; 58 human subthemes
evidence_records.Document length: short-form forum posts; lengths not reported
evidence_records.Language: English implied but not explicitly reported
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: publicly accessible health-worker forum discourse; authors describe posts as anonymized
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-3.5 for theme generation and GPT-4 for comparison; exact model snapshots not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Structured system/user messages ask for themes and subthemes; GPT-4 receives both human and model themes and four comparison criteria. Multimedia Appendix 1 provides prompt details, but main-text temperature and seed values are not stated.
evidence_records.Agent roles: GPT-3.5 theme/subtheme generator; GPT-4 evaluator of alignment, convergence, coherence and complementarity
evidence_records.Human role: Two coders label topics, resolve disagreements and derive subthemes; two authors independently classify human–LLM agreement and adjudicate; humans compare GPT-4 judgments with their classifications.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: LDA topic represented by its top 10 posts
evidence_records.Generated outputs: human themes, GPT themes/subthemes, seven-category comparison labels and four GPT-4 evaluation attributes
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Top posts ground each topic, and selected examples reveal one-post subthemes; complete post–theme provenance and the corpus are unavailable.
evidence_records.Baselines: two-human topic labels and subthemes versus GPT-3.5; human comparison categories versus GPT-4 self-evaluation
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one reported generation/evaluation per topic; seed is said to be specified but its value, reruns and order tests are not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: LDA coherence; raw human agreement percentages; ad hoc seven-category percentage; GPT-4 binary alignment/convergence/coherence/complementarity
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Two authors independently classify 310 human–LLM pairs and resolve disagreement, but no pre-adjudication reliability coefficient is reported for the seven-category scale.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two human topic coders and two author comparators; expertise is not characterized in detail; GPT-4 also judges outputs from GPT-3.5
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: Human theme labels: 68% initial agreement, 94% after a second round, remaining 18/310 resolved jointly. Reported 79.7% is not an inter-rater coefficient.
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive counts and percentages; no uncertainty intervals or chance-corrected agreement for the main comparison
evidence_records.Principal results: Authors classify 247/310 (79.7%) as agreement, comprising 95 taxonomic matches, 101 subtheme matches and 51 cases where the LLM diverged but humans judged the topic low-coherence. GPT-4 overaccepted coherence: 49/51 human-low-coherence cases and 29/30 overly broad cases; it also marked 87% of the overly broad set complementary.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: automation/scalability is asserted but no measured time, labor or cost is reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Authors deemed IRB review unnecessary because the study used publicly available anonymized forum posts; contributor expectations and quotation-searchability are not discussed.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Multimedia Appendix 1 contains prompts and modeling/comparison details; no data or executable code package reported
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: single forum, one short-form English context, GPT-3.5/GPT-4 only, simple prompts and no long-form evaluation
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Methods state 15/310 (16.5%) low-coherence topics, whereas Table 2/results correctly use 51/310. The 79.7% “reliability” category includes divergent LLM themes when humans found the input cluster incoherent, so it is not ordinary agreement. GPT-4 evaluates another OpenAI model and force-fits coherence/complementarity from isolated posts, undermining independence.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Uses the nurse-forum corpus and LDA pipeline reported in the authors' 2023 JMIR Nursing article; the LLM interpretation layer is the new contribution.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Provides a warning case for evaluator independence, clear denominators and category semantics. An ARR system should not allow a model-generated broad theme or a low-quality source cluster to count as “agreement” without human source-grounded review.

LLM-Assisted Thematic Analysis: Opportunities, Limitations, and Recommendations. arXiv:2511.14528v1. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17443995.
evidence_records.Title: LLM-Assisted Thematic Analysis: Opportunities, Limitations, and Recommendations
evidence_records.Authors: Tatiane Ornelas; Allysson Allex Araújo; Júlia Araújo; Marina Araújo; Bianca Trinkenreich; Marcos Kalinowski
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: not peer reviewed in the inspected version
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1 posted 2025-11-18; reports an ISERN 2025 workshop and cites a separate Zenodo artifact
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: ISERN 2025 LLM-assisted thematic-analysis workshop and Zenodo artifact; illustrative example comes from an ongoing separate interview study
evidence_records.Research objective: Elicit experienced software-engineering researchers' views on opportunities, limitations and safeguards for LLM-assisted open coding, theme generation and theme review, and present a five-phase/seven-step collaboration process.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: structured reflective workshop and LLM-assisted thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Twenty-five ISERN participants worked in five groups for 30 minutes on color-coded A2 canvases after a process demonstration. Authors transcribed each post-it, organized it by phase/category and descriptively grouped recurring ideas. A separate illustrative example shows GPT-4 coding authentic excerpts and humans validating codes/themes, but it does not report a performance evaluation.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: workshop synthesis is structured deductively by three phases and three color categories, with descriptive inductive grouping within cells; illustrative coding is presented as inductive
evidence_records.Domain: empirical software engineering / qualitative research methodology
evidence_records.Dataset name: five ISERN workshop canvases plus a small authentic excerpt illustration from an ongoing study of software engineers' interpersonal/reflection abilities
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: workshop materials and consolidated spreadsheet are associated with Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17443995; underlying interview corpus is not public or fully described
evidence_records.Number of documents: 5 completed A2 canvases; number of post-its and underlying interview documents not reported
evidence_records.Number of participants: 25 workshop participants; participant count for the illustrative ongoing interview study not reported
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: five group canvases and an unspecified subset of authentic interview excerpts; no word/post-it total
evidence_records.Document length: 60-minute workshop with 30-minute group-canvas phase; interview excerpt lengths vary and are not summarized
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: workshop reflections and anonymized interview excerpts labeled by participant IDs; ethics/privacy procedures are not reported
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4; exact snapshot, access date and configuration not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Modular prompts specify research context, data source, task, quality criteria and tabular output for open codes, candidate themes and redundant-code review; exact complete prompts are not reproduced in the paper
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: no fine-tuning or RAG in the illustrative example
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single LLM used sequentially across human-validation gates
evidence_records.Agent roles: open coder, theme grouper and redundancy reviewer
evidence_records.Human role: Researchers familiarize themselves with all data, review every generated code, validate/refine themes, reject harmful consolidations and write the report; workshop participants provide methodological reflections.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: workshop post-it for the empirical study; quote/code/theme for the illustrative workflow
evidence_records.Generated outputs: opportunity/risk/recommendation groupings; code-description-quote tables; candidate themes; semantic consolidation proposals; a seven-step human–LLM workflow
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Illustrative tables retain quote and participant identifiers through code/theme stages; workshop post-its are in an artifact, but paper results do not report item counts by finding.
evidence_records.Baselines: no model-performance baseline; participants recommend manual coding and multi-model comparison as safeguards
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: not reported for GPT-4; one 60-minute workshop with five simultaneous groups
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: none; the workshop synthesis explicitly does not quantify consensus or model performance
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Senior empirical-software-engineering researchers discuss a conceptual workflow; this is expert reflection, not evaluation of actual model outputs. Authors validate the separate example internally.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: 25 ISERN researchers described as experienced/senior; exact demographics and expertise distribution not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not reported
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: structured descriptive synthesis only
evidence_records.Principal results: Participants saw efficiency, scale and alternative taxonomies, but emphasized loss of familiarization/context, instability, bias, overproduction and review burden. Safeguards included manual engagement, human validation, multiple models, documented prompts/versions/interventions and prompt literacy.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: participants perceived potential time savings; no measured time or cost
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: no ethics approval, consent process or privacy protocol is reported for the workshop or illustrative interview excerpts
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Zenodo artifact DOI 10.5281/zenodo.17443995 with workshop materials/consolidated spreadsheet; no executable system, exact model snapshot or complete underlying interview corpus
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: single situated workshop with a focused group of senior empirical-SE researchers; not statistically generalizable and not a model-performance study
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The “concrete example” lacks corpus size, model configuration, reruns and outcome measures and should not be treated as empirical evidence that the workflow preserves interpretive depth. Workshop expectations about efficiency and model behavior are perceptions, not observed effects.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: The example is drawn from an ongoing author study and may later form a separate publication family; this record should not be merged with that future empirical report without exact-family review.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Supports governance requirements—human familiarization, validation gates, traceable quotes and intervention logs—but supplies no comparative accuracy or stability evidence for ARR ranking.

evidence_records.Full citation: Oksanen, Joel, Andrés Lucero, and Perttu Hämäläinen. 2025. LLMCode: Evaluating and Enhancing Researcher-AI Alignment in Qualitative Analysis. arXiv:2504.16671v1.
evidence_records.Title: LLMCode: Evaluating and Enhancing Researcher-AI Alignment in Qualitative Analysis
evidence_records.Authors: Joel Oksanen; Andrés Lucero; Perttu Hämäläinen
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: not peer reviewed; manuscript says “submitted to ACM”
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1; inspected manuscript has anonymous-review GitHub placeholder and placeholder ACM DOI 10.1145/nnnnnnn.nnnnnnn, so no archival publication is established
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: LLMCode toolkit and two associated designer studies
evidence_records.Research objective: Develop IoU and modified Hausdorff distance measures for human–LLM coding alignment, evaluate GPT-4o in-context learning of individual coding perspectives, and study reciprocal influence during interactive refinement.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive qualitative coding in research-for-design plus reflexive thematic analysis of user feedback
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: LLMCode sequentially generates span highlights and open codes while accumulating a codebook. Study 1 has 19 game-design students manually code up to 200 Reddit texts, then uses their annotations as examples/baselines. Study 2 has seven designers manually code data and perform two further example/prompt iterations against the same validation annotations. Logs are quantified with IoU/MHD and the first author reflexively analyzes surveys and 428 minutes of think-aloud data.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: nominally inductive generation; as examples accumulate, performance increasingly reflects deductive reuse of a stabilizing codebook
evidence_records.Domain: research for design / HCI / game-design research
evidence_records.Dataset name: 19 participant-created Reddit research corpora and seven designer datasets (three user-provided, four using transcripts from three service-design interviews)
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: source Reddit data and participant annotations are not deposited in the anonymous manuscript; some Study 2 data were participant-owned/restricted
evidence_records.Number of documents: Study 1 participants each manually annotated up to 200 texts; Study 2 document counts vary and are not fully reported
evidence_records.Number of participants: 19 master's game-design students plus 7 designers (26 total)
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: Study 1 manual subsets range from 12 to 283 texts per participant in Table 2, with 6–68 codes; Study 2 produced 428 minutes of think-aloud data, 149 quotations and 63 codes
evidence_records.Document length: Study 1 Reddit texts; Study 2 sessions about 90 minutes; source-text lengths not reported
evidence_records.Language: not explicitly reported; manuscript and quoted material are in English
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: participant-provided and online discussion data; the paper tells participants to bring data only when permitted but reports no formal privacy/ethics protocol
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4o and text-embedding-3-large; snapshots, temperature and other inference settings not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Sequential inductive coding with Markdown span annotations, accumulating codebook and few-shot positive/negative examples; users can edit instructions and examples; full inductive prompt appears in the appendix
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: in-context learning only; no weight fine-tuning
evidence_records.Agent roles: span highlighter/open coder, code-description generator and broader-theme grouper
evidence_records.Human role: Humans manually create the baseline, select examples, change prompt instructions, visually compare annotations and may revise their own codes in response to the model; researchers analyze logs and participant reflections.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: text span/highlight and attached open code; participant-level code sets and example-set iterations
evidence_records.Generated outputs: highlighted source spans, open codes/codebook, broader themes, IoU/MHD alignment scores and interaction logs
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Generated annotations are anchored to verbatim text spans and discrepancy checks try to reconstruct altered source text; the interface displays model and human spans side by side.
evidence_records.Baselines: participant manual annotations; randomly sampled example sets matched in size to human selections for Study 2
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: Study 1 learning curves on 11 eligible participant datasets and extrapolation on 8; Study 2 uses three human-curated iterations and five random example sets per iteration; stochastic model reruns/seeds are not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: span Intersection over Union; embedding-based modified Hausdorff distance between code sets; Pearson correlation; code-discovery rate
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: 26 user-study participants provide manual annotations, surveys and think-aloud feedback; model outputs are compared to each participant's changing personal baseline rather than an independent gold interpretation.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: 19 game-design students with varied analysis experience and 7 designers; first author conducts reflexive thematic analysis, with no second analytic evaluator reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not applicable to individualized reflexive coding; no reliability statistic for the first-author thematic analysis
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: learning curves with least-squares asymptotic fit, Pearson r=.53 for example-to-target versus model-to-human code distance, metric trajectories and five-sample random baselines; uncertainty/significance tests are limited
evidence_records.Principal results: More examples improved mean IoU and reduced MHD, but gains largely tracked code reuse and codebook stabilization. When target codes were unlike examples, model–human distance worsened (Pearson r=.53). Human-curated iteration improved later IoU relative to random selection, while users also changed their own coding after seeing model output.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: efficiency/scale benefits are asserted; no end-to-end time or cost comparison is reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: voluntary/unincentivized Study 1 and recruitment details are reported; the manuscript does not report IRB/ethics approval, consent language, data-governance protocol or a formal privacy analysis
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: appendix prompt and detailed interface/method; GitHub is described as open source but the anonymous manuscript replaces the URL with “<link omitted for anonymous review>”
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: in-context learning mainly captures surface/codebook reuse; user difficulty understanding examples; risk of overfitting; Study 2 lacks a separate test set; researcher coding shifts during iteration
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Study 2 optimizes against and visually exposes the same validation annotations without a held-out test set. Because users revise their own baseline after seeing model outputs, improved alignment can reflect human anchoring rather than model learning. MHD is model-dependent semantic proximity, not interpretive validity.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Builds on the authors' prior LLM coding workflow and related Research-for-Design studies; no duplicate archival version verified.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Strong support for quote-span provenance, held-out testing and monitoring human-baseline drift. IoU/MHD can diagnose alignment but should be secondary to plural, blind, source-grounded human assessment.

evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: inductive theme generation constrained by prompt-requested domains and a fixed consensus/clustering procedure
evidence_records.Dataset name: one semi-structured ketamine art-therapy therapist interview
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: full transcript is public in the project GitHub repository
evidence_records.Number of participants: 1 therapist
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 28,377 characters and 173 lines
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: clinical/practice interview about therapy; public transcript, but consent/publication-governance details are not reported beyond thanking the therapist
evidence_records.Model family: Google Gemini, OpenAI GPT and Anthropic Claude
evidence_records.Exact model/version: Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet; provider snapshots and API dates not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Custom JSON prompt requests core themes, therapist methodology, client experiences, future outlook, supporting quotes and a {seed} run identifier; temperature .7 and six numeric seed values are reported
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: none; all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings are run locally for similarity/clustering
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single-agent repetitions within each model, then cross-model comparison; not a deliberative multi-agent system
evidence_records.Agent roles: independent theme generator and deterministic consensus aggregator
evidence_records.Human role: Authors select the corpus, prompt, threshold and metrics and interpret outputs; no human thematic analysis or independent theme-validity judgment is used.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: generated theme description and its presence/absence across runs
evidence_records.Generated outputs: themes with supporting quotes, pairwise kappa/cosine matrices, consensus theme clusters and frequency labels
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Prompt requests supporting quotes and the transcript/output examples are public, but reported aggregate metrics are not linked to a human-validated source-to-theme audit.
evidence_records.Baselines: three LLM families compared with one another; no manual coder, established codebook or external-validity baseline
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: 6 per model (18 total) with reported values 42, 123, 456, 789, 1011 and 1213 at temperature .7
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: pairwise Cohen's kappa on theme presence/absence, all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cosine similarity, >=.70 semantic clustering, >=50% consensus frequency and Pearson correlation between kappa and cosine
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: none for theme correctness, completeness, depth, cultural validity or source fidelity
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: authors only; one therapist supplied the dataset but is not reported as an output evaluator
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: No human IRR. Mean inter-run kappa is reported as .907 Gemini, .853 GPT-4o and .842 Claude; these are model self-consistency statistics.
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: 15 pairwise comparisons per model, mean/range summaries, Pearson r=.97 between kappa and cosine; no confidence intervals or held-out validation
evidence_records.Principal results: Gemini produced 6 consensus themes, GPT-4o 5 and Claude 4; only 1–2 themes per model reached 5/6 runs. Reported kappa/cosine were .907/95.3%, .853/92.6% and .842/92.1%, respectively; cross-model theme overlap is described as 60–70%.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: claims $0.15–$0.20 per transcript versus $20–$40 human coding and table estimates of $3–$6 versus $400–$800 for 20 documents; derivation and equivalent synthesis/review labor are not empirically demonstrated
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: local preprocessing and API-key handling are described, but raw transcripts are sent to providers at analysis initiation. Consent, IRB status, data license and clinical privacy review for the public therapist transcript are not reported.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: code, live app, transcript and examples: https://github.com/NileshArnaiya/LLM-Thematic-Analysis-Tool and https://azalab-llm-tool.vercel.app/
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: single dataset; cultural/domain bounds; prompt dependence; inability to perform reflexivity or ethical judgment; need for human oversight and future human comparison
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: High internal consistency is not external validity. Kappa requires a stable item/category universe, but theme equivalence is first induced by an embedding threshold; this makes the chance-corrected interpretation unclear. Putting {seed} in a prompt is not proof that every provider honors a stochastic seed. Claims of rigorous validation and human-comparable reliability exceed one transcript with no human baseline.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Current v2 belongs in the 2026 stream; exact-title/version deduplication is required before master merge.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Useful implementation for repeated-run instability and consensus displays, but a negative example for treating self-consistency as validity. ARR should pair such runs with blind human source-grounded evaluation and preserve minority interpretations.

evidence_records.Full citation: Wen, Shuide, Beier Ku, Teng Wang, Mingyang Zou, and Yang Yang. 2025. Neo-Grounded Theory: A Methodological Innovation Integrating High-Dimensional Vector Clustering and Multi-Agent Collaboration for Qualitative Research. arXiv:2509.25244v1.
evidence_records.Title: Neo-Grounded Theory: A Methodological Innovation Integrating High-Dimensional Vector Clustering and Multi-Agent Collaboration for Qualitative Research
evidence_records.Authors: Shuide Wen; Beier Ku; Teng Wang; Mingyang Zou; Yang Yang
evidence_records.Publication history notes: arXiv v1; no journal/conference version, DOI or code archive identified
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official arXiv full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: visually impaired gamers dataset previously analyzed in Yue et al. (2024); NGT is a new claimed method on the same corpus
evidence_records.Research objective: Propose Neo-Grounded Theory, combining vector clustering, parallel LLM coding agents and human prompt refinement, and compare it with traditional grounded-theory and ChatGPT-4 Turbo analyses.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: grounded theory / Neo-Grounded Theory with computational emergence, distributed cognition and augmented theoretical sensitivity
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Eight Chinese interview transcripts are segmented, embedded with text-embedding-3-small, hierarchically clustered and distributed across 8–12 concurrent coding agents for open/axial/selective coding and integration. One automated and one expert-prompt-refined NGT output are compared with a previously/manual baseline and ChatGPT-4 Turbo. Three LLMs, rather than human experts, assign quality scores.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: claimed inductive grounded theory; clustering thresholds, staged prompts and expert-refined tension/contradiction instructions impose substantial structure
evidence_records.Domain: disability, gaming, well-being and social participation
evidence_records.Dataset name: eight semi-structured interviews with visually impaired gamers, originally collected February–March 2022
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: restricted secondary interview data; no transcript deposit reported
evidence_records.Number of participants: 8 visually impaired gamers, ages 18–41
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: about 40,000 Chinese characters
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: disability and well-being interviews; deidentified secondary data
evidence_records.Model family: OpenAI GPT/embeddings and unspecified NGT coding LLM agents; Claude and DeepSeek used as evaluators
evidence_records.Exact model/version: ChatGPT-4 Turbo “current as of January 2024”; text-embedding-3-small; evaluator labels ChatGPT-5.0, Claude Opus 4.1 and DeepSeek V3.1; exact NGT agent model and snapshots are not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Three-stage coding prompts, semantic-cluster distribution and JSON output; Exp. 2 adds expert instructions to focus on tensions, contradictions and divergent pathways. Only brief example prompts are shown.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: no reported weight tuning; human prompt refinement and fixed clustering threshold
evidence_records.Agent roles: parallel cluster-level open/axial/selective coders and cross-cluster theory integrator; exact role prompts and model assignments not reported
evidence_records.Human role: Two researchers provide the claimed manual baseline; an expert reviews Exp. 1 and refines Exp. 2 prompts; original participants perform unspecified member checking where possible; a methodologist reviews an unspecified audit subset.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: 50–200-word semantic segment, cluster, code, subtheme and theoretical framework
evidence_records.Generated outputs: 268–289 open codes, 42–56 subthemes, 7–9 main themes, theoretical diagrams, quality scores and cost/time estimates
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Authors claim complete audit trails and source grounding, but no trail, transcript-to-code map, full prompts, outputs or code is supplied for inspection.
evidence_records.Baselines: traditional manual NVivo grounded theory, ChatGPT-4 Turbo, automated NGT Exp. 1 and human-refined NGT Exp. 2
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: one reported output per condition; no stochastic reruns, seeds, order tests or threshold ablation
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: processing time, cost, code/theme counts, claimed Jaccard and semantic alignment, coverage/redundancy, LLM-scored six-dimension quality and Krippendorff alpha among three LLM evaluators
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: The main quality table explicitly replaces human experts with three LLM judges. Elsewhere the paper claims multiple human experts, member checking and a methodologist audit but supplies no counts, judgments or results.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: three LLM judges for reported quality scores; vague/unquantified human experts, participants and methodologist for other checks
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: LLM-evaluator Krippendorff alpha=.91; manual baseline claims h > .85 (apparently a typesetting error for kappa) without denominator or calculation details
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive single-run comparisons; no uncertainty or inferential testing
evidence_records.Principal results: Reported total times are 504 hours manual, 24 hours ChatGPT, .5 hours automated NGT and 3 hours human-refined NGT. LLM judges score NGT Exp. 2 .904 versus manual .883. Reported manual–NGT Jaccard is 75.4% and semantic alignment 83%; NGT Exp. 2 produces 268 codes, 52 subthemes and 9 themes.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: Results table reports $12,800 manual, $425 ChatGPT and $95 NGT (99.3% reduction), while the abstract reports a 95.8% reduction and later prose says 96%; assumptions include $50/hour and projected sublinear/logarithmic scaling without empirical scale tests.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Source approval is reported as Renmin University School of Journalism and Communication #20220028, with secondary-analysis consent and 50 RMB compensation; deidentification, encryption/access/deletion controls and respectful framing are described.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: no code, data, complete prompts, audit trail or output package reported
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: single domain, Chinese-only, modest 40,000-character corpus, theoretical-evaluation subjectivity, loss of metaphor/narrative/cultural nuance and technical gatekeeping
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The reported primary quality advantage is an LLM-as-judge self-evaluation with no human outcome table. Methods contradict themselves about whether human experts evaluated outputs. Cost-reduction percentages conflict; clustering is “fixed at .52” but later sensitivity is described for .80–.90; logarithmic scaling is asserted from one corpus. The paper does not identify the core NGT coding model or enable reproduction.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Reuses the Yue et al. visually impaired gamer corpus and its manual/ChatGPT analyses; dependency should be recorded rather than counted as an independent dataset replication.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: A low-confidence cautionary case: it motivates agent audit trails and human refinement, but its headline quality, novelty, speed and cost claims should not inform ARR ranking without reproducible runs, human-blind evaluation and dependency adjustment.

evidence_records.Title: Online extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (EFAST) course enhanced knowledge and perceived confidence among medical trainees during the COVID-19 pandemic disaster
evidence_records.Authors: Arif Alper Cevik; Fikri M. Abu-Zidan
evidence_records.Publication history notes: received 2024-10-23, accepted 2025-03-31, published 2025-04-09; PMCID PMC11980233, PMID 40205423
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; publisher/PMC full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: applied EFAST-course evaluation; LLM analysis is one secondary qualitative component
evidence_records.Research objective: Evaluate an online EFAST course's effects on knowledge and perceived confidence; use ChatGPT/Custom-GPT and NotebookLM to assist analysis of open-ended course feedback.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: Braun and Clarke six-step inductive thematic analysis with human, Custom-GPT and NotebookLM “triangulation”
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Authors cleaned/anonymized 220 post-course comments, uploaded CSV data to ChatGPT-4o, converted them to PDF, configured a Custom-GPT around Braun–Clarke steps, and uploaded the PDF to Custom-GPT and NotebookLM. The paper reports 14 codes and three themes but no system-specific outputs, comparison procedure or adjudication trace.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: claimed inductive; Custom-GPT is configured with a predefined six-step methodological frame
evidence_records.Dataset name: open-ended post-course EFAST feedback from a global online course
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: not available; data-availability statement says no datasets were generated or analyzed, contradicting the reported survey dataset
evidence_records.Number of participants: 220 feedback respondents among 938 exit-survey completers; 1,758 enrolled and 1,515 started
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 220 comments; 14 codes and 3 themes
evidence_records.Document length: short open-ended survey responses; lengths not reported
evidence_records.Language: course and feedback appear to be English; language is not explicitly reported for the comments
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: anonymized educational survey responses; user IDs were removed after pre/post matching
evidence_records.Exact model/version: ChatGPT-4o, a study-specific Custom-GPT, and NotebookLM; snapshots/access dates not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Custom-GPT objectives and Braun–Clarke steps were configured, but exact instructions, prompts and output constraints are not supplied
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: Custom-GPT configuration only; no weight fine-tuning reported
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: two independent tools plus human input, described as triangulation rather than an integrated multi-agent workflow
evidence_records.Agent roles: data-format converter, inductive thematic coder and emergent-theme assistant
evidence_records.Human role: Two authors jointly analyzed data, established the Custom-GPT objective/method and compared human input with two model tools; division of coding, validation and adjudication labor is not described.
evidence_records.Generated outputs: 14 codes and three themes: Content Delivery and Engagement, Technical and Structural Improvements, and Positive Learning Experience
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Results include selected participant quotations labeled only by country, but no complete comment–code–theme table or tool-specific provenance.
evidence_records.Baselines: claimed comparison among human manual input, Custom-GPT and NotebookLM; no separate outputs or concordance results are reported
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: none for qualitative/LLM analysis; quantitative course outcomes use Wilcoxon tests and Cohen's d but do not evaluate the LLM method
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: authors jointly interpret and report final themes; there is no blinded assessment of model outputs
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two authors; qualitative-method expertise and separate coding roles not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not reported
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: no qualitative-analysis statistics; 220/938 (23.5%) exit-survey respondents supplied comments
evidence_records.Principal results: The LLM-assisted analysis yields 14 codes and three broad themes about engagement, technical/structural improvements and positive experience. No evidence distinguishes which tool generated or changed any code/theme, or whether triangulation improved accuracy.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: paper asserts improved processing efficiency but reports no qualitative-analysis time, cost or human-review burden
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: UAE University deemed the education evaluation exempt (ERS_2020_6130); surveys were optional, identifiers removed and database access restricted
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: no prompts, code, model settings, comments or audit outputs; the data-availability statement is internally inaccurate
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: authors note only 23.5% supplied feedback and possible response bias, but do not discuss LLM-specific validity, instability, privacy or model dependence
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The triangulation and “increased analytical accuracy” claims are unsupported because model-specific outputs, human comparison and disagreements are absent. Broad positive themes can reflect response/self-selection bias. Upload pathway and provider data governance are not described. “No datasets ... analyzed” is false on the face of the methods.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: No related LLM-method publication identified; primary contribution is course evaluation rather than qualitative-computing methodology.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: An applied reporting-failure case showing why ARR should require exact prompts/models, separate system outputs, human adjudication, full provenance and truthful data availability before an LLM-assisted thematic analysis is auditable.

evidence_records.Full citation: Liu, Xiner, Andres Felipe Zambrano, Ryan S. Baker, Amanda Barany, Jaclyn Ocumpaugh, Jiayi Zhang, Maciej Pankiewicz, Nidhi Nasiar, and Zhanlan Wei. 2025. Qualitative Coding with GPT-4: Where It Works Better. Journal of Learning Analytics 12(1):169–185. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8575.
evidence_records.Title: Qualitative Coding with GPT-4: Where it Works Better
evidence_records.Authors: Xiner Liu; Andres Felipe Zambrano; Ryan S. Baker; Amanda Barany; Jaclyn Ocumpaugh; Jiayi Zhang; Maciej Pankiewicz; Nidhi Nasiar; Zhanlan Wei
evidence_records.Publication history notes: submitted 2024-07-27, accepted 2025-02-11 and published 2025-03-17
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official journal full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: Three educational-dataset study drawing codebooks/data from Barany et al. (2024), Yi et al. (2020), Pinto et al. (2023) and Zambrano et al. (2024)
evidence_records.Research objective: Determine which zero-shot, few-shot, context and embedding strategies best reproduce human qualitative codes across constructs with different clarity, concreteness, objectivity, granularity and specificity.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: automated qualitative coding with GPT-4 across three educational datasets
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Researchers begin with previously or newly inductively developed codebooks, resolve human disagreements to one reference label per unit, then run separate binary 0/1 GPT-4 classifiers for each predefined construct. The evaluation is supervised/deductive multi-label classification, not emergent thematic interpretation.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid upstream codebook development; the evaluated GPT task is deductive binary code application
evidence_records.Domain: education: Grade 9 math tutoring, middle-school astronomy/Minecraft observations and university introductory programming
evidence_records.Dataset name: Saga Algebra I tutoring transcripts; WHIMC observations; RunCode C# debugging submissions
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: Study 3 raw deidentified data and coded versions are linked for sharing; Studies 1–2 are not deposited in the paper
evidence_records.Number of documents: 4 tutoring transcripts; 200 WHIMC observations evaluated; 44,448 RunCode submissions in the source corpus, with the exact evaluated conditional-statement subset not reported
evidence_records.Number of participants: 6 ninth-grade tutoring students, 76 WHIMC learners and 169 RunCode students; human coder counts are two in Studies 1–2 and underreported for Study 3
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: Study 1: 990 instructor lines; Study 2: 200 observations; Study 3: source corpus 44,448 submissions over 146 tasks, evaluation-subset denominator not reported
evidence_records.Document length: Study 1 has four 60-minute sessions; Study 2 observations are short posts; Study 3 submissions often exceed 50 code lines but only changed lines are sent
evidence_records.Language: English natural-language data; C# source code from a Polish course
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: deidentified education data involving minors and university students; Study 3 sharing is described as deidentified
evidence_records.Exact model/version: gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09 and text-embedding-3-small
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Temperature 0, default remaining parameters; construct definition for zero-shot, annotated positive examples for few-shot, positive/negative examples for programming, and study/three-line context for tutoring. Prompts were iteratively tuned on separate validation data; a .60 embedding threshold was selected on 100 WHIMC lines.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: no weight fine-tuning; iterative prompt engineering and example selection
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single-model binary classifier run independently for each construct
evidence_records.Agent roles: deductive code applier; embedding similarity is used for one continuing-discussion construct
evidence_records.Human role: Researchers develop/refine codebooks, double-code and adjudicate reference labels, tune prompts and examples, rate construct properties and inspect errors.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: tutor utterance line, student observation, or changed lines between consecutive code submissions
evidence_records.Generated outputs: binary label per construct/unit, kappa/precision/recall, construct-property ratings and method recommendations
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Each prediction maps to a source unit and code; error examples are quoted, but complete predictions/prompts and most source data are not public.
evidence_records.Baselines: human adjudicated labels; zero-shot versus several few-shot/context strategies and one embedding method
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: Study 1 and Study 2 coding were run three times and averaged; Study 3 repetition count is not explicitly reported; random seeds are not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Cohen's kappa, precision, recall, construct frequency, Cronbach alpha for a questionable property-rating aggregation and Spearman correlations
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Two researchers independently code/adjudicate Studies 1–2; eleven qualitative researchers rate ten Study 1 constructs. Study 3 human-reference construction is not described with equal detail.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two coders in Study 1, two in Study 2, eleven construct-property raters; Study 3 coder number/expertise underreported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: Study 1 human–human kappa .24–.87 by construct; Study 2 .73–.97; Study 3 .32–1.00. Disagreements were adjudicated before human–GPT evaluation.
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: per-construct kappa/precision/recall averaged over runs; Spearman correlations on only ten Study 1 constructs; Cronbach alpha .75–.93 across unlike rating dimensions
evidence_records.Principal results: At least one prompting approach reached kappa >=.70 for 25/34 constructs. Context helped temporally dependent tutoring codes; few-shot examples sometimes overgeneralized; embedding performed best for continuing discussion (kappa .93). GPT struggled when humans disagreed and on less concrete/context-dependent constructs.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: API workflow is described as more efficient than chat copy/paste, but no measured time or cost is reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: No IRB, consent, data-use approval or privacy-governance statement is reported despite deidentified data from minors and students
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: paper prints representative prompts and links Study 3 deidentified raw/coded data; executable code, complete predictions and Studies 1–2 data are not reported
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: binary one-construct-at-a-time design; prompt-method effectiveness varies; few-shot overgeneralization; context can add noise; need other LLMs, multi-code prompts and more complex constructs
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Prompt/example/context choices were iteratively optimized, but validation/test denominators and leakage controls are incompletely reported; the embedding threshold used half of Study 2 data. The narrative prints Questioning zero-shot kappa as −.91 while Table 2 and discussion support +.91. Adjudicated single ground truth suppresses legitimate interpretive plurality, and Cronbach alpha is misapplied to six distinct construct-property dimensions.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Study 1 directly reuses a GPT-refined codebook from Barany et al. (2024); Studies 2–3 refine earlier codebooks. Dependency-adjusted synthesis should not count these as three independent model-development replications.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Material evidence for construct-stratified evaluation, exact model snapshots, repeated runs and context ablations. It favors source-level kappa/precision/recall for deductive coding, while highlighting leakage, plurality and denominator requirements for ARR.

evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Strong design guidance on stable source IDs, local processing, negative/minority cases, version logs, and limiting automation to stable/indexical tasks.

evidence_records.Title: Artificial Intelligence to Support Qualitative Data Analysis: Promises, Approaches, Pitfalls
evidence_records.Authors: David A. Cook; Shiphra Ginsburg; Adam P. Sawatsky; Ayelet Kuper; Jonathan D. D'Angelo
evidence_records.Publication type: peer-reviewed journal article combining an exploratory case report, limited scoping review, and critical appraisal
evidence_records.Publication history notes: Received 2024-10-04; revised through 2025-04-04; accepted 2025-04-14; published online 2025-06-25; October 2025 issue.
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official publisher full HTML inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: standalone case experiment plus scoping review; no duplicate report identified in the 2025 screen
evidence_records.Research objective: Critically appraise how AI can support qualitative data analysis through an out-of-the-box ChatGPT-4 experiment, a limited scoping review, and methodological/ethical synthesis.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: qualitative data analysis case report plus scoping review of AI-supported QDA
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: The authors iteratively prompted ChatGPT-4 in February 2024 to reanalyze three existing narrative datasets and documented task successes/failures; separately, one reviewer searched six sources in February/May 2024, screened 483 items, and extracted 130 included publications.

evidence_records.Public or restricted data: mixed; dataset 3 came from an open repository, while datasets 1–2 were existing author-held/unpublished narrative data
evidence_records.Number of documents: 30 student response pairs; 211 physician free-text responses; 3 interview transcripts selected from a 30-interview repository dataset
evidence_records.Number of participants: 30 third-year medical students; 211 physicians; 3 interviewed researchers in the analyzed subset
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 1,380 words; 7,419 words; 19,207 words, respectively
evidence_records.Document length: dataset 3 transcripts were approximately 6,000 words each; exact lengths for individual short responses not reported
evidence_records.Language: English for the case experiment; review included any language and used automated translation for Spanish, Tagalog, and Chinese papers
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: existing narrative human-participant data; the article discusses confidentiality risks but does not report transmitting direct identifiers
evidence_records.Exact model/version: ChatGPT-4 as available in February 2024; API snapshot, temperature, seed, and system configuration not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: iterative natural-language prompts moving from multistep whole-task requests to progressively clarified/simplified requests; verbatim prompts are in Supplemental Digital Appendix 1
evidence_records.Agent roles: summarizer, inductive theme generator, keyword/theme counter, sentiment labeler, quotation selector, and attempted visualizer/cross-theme analyst
evidence_records.Human role: authors selected data/tasks, iteratively revised prompts, manually checked outputs against source texts, judged usefulness, conducted the review, and retained interpretive responsibility
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: short narrative response, interview transcript, proposed theme/code, and supporting quotation
evidence_records.Generated outputs: summaries, themes/categories, prevalence counts, sentiment labels, quotations, word-cloud attempts, and task-specific narrative outputs
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Authors manually compared generated outputs with input data and report concrete failures; the supplement preserves prompts, but no machine-readable output-to-source audit package was verified.
evidence_records.Baselines: source texts and author judgment; no independent human thematic analysis was systematically scored against the model for all tasks
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: multiple iterative prompts and repeat attempts; exact run count and seeds not reported; authors observed widely divergent rerun outputs
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: none for the case experiment; the scoping review reports descriptive counts/percentages
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: informal expert inspection of output accuracy, task fulfillment, quotation support, and utility; not a blinded or preregistered evaluation
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: five author-methodologists/medical educators; task-by-task evaluator assignment and independent ratings not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not calculated for the ChatGPT experiment; scoping-review screening/extraction was performed by one author
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive counts only; no inferential testing
evidence_records.Principal results: Brief summaries were accurate, but initial prompts failed for all other attempted tasks. Iteration rescued some counting/summarization tasks, while thematic analysis, highlighting, word-tree diagrams, and cross-theme insights remained unsatisfactory. Errors included impossible counts, unsupported/reused quotations, superficial catch-all categories, hallucinated word-cloud terms, failed instruction following, and unstable reruns. The review retained 130 of 483 records, including 104 original studies.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: no timed or monetary comparison; the context-window forced selection of only 3 of 30 long interviews
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Substantial discussion of consent, confidentiality, commercial model retention, reidentification, fraud, workforce effects, and preserving a human in the loop; case-study ethics approval/consent status for reuse is not separately reported in the article text inspected.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Supplemental Digital Appendices include prompts, review details, and the included-study list; dataset 3 is repository-sourced, but complete experiment outputs/code/model settings were not provided.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Authors call the case experiment extemporaneous and attribute failure partly to their limited prompt sophistication; the review had one reviewer, limited extraction, and possible omissions; model capabilities change rapidly.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: No independent blinded reference analysis or quantitative scoring, author-selected tasks/subsets, uncertain run accounting, and an unspecified ChatGPT-4 snapshot limit performance inference. The review’s broad definition of AI/QDA is wider than this review’s LLM-centered scope.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Synthesizes 130 earlier AI-QDA publications and directly tests three previously collected datasets; not an independent reanalysis benchmark family with a fixed gold standard.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: High-value negative evidence: require atomic prompts, source-linked outputs, explicit context-window accounting, reruns, deterministic arithmetic checks, and expert human adjudication before treating fluent output as analysis.

evidence_records.Title: Data Plus Theory Equals Codebook: Leveraging LLMs for Human-AI Codebook Development
evidence_records.Authors: Andres Felipe Zambrano; Jiayi Zhang; Jaclyn Ocumpaugh; Xiner Liu; Luc Paquette; Conrad Borchers; Zhanlan Wei; Ryan S. Baker; Amanda Barany; Yiqiu Zhou; Jeffrey Ginger

evidence_records.Research objective: Test whether GPT-4o can support theory-informed qualitative codebook development and how varying the amount of theory supplied changes practical utility and theoretical alignment.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: human–AI, theory-driven qualitative codebook development across self-regulated learning and interest-development studies
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Study 1 combined named SRL theories, 955 think-aloud utterances, GPT-4o-generated constructs/examples, and first/second-author consolidation. Study 2 generated 12 codebooks from four theory-context prompt conditions (three runs each), consolidated them, and had five coauthor experts score seven qualities.

evidence_records.Dataset name: SRL think-aloud corpus from three intelligent tutoring systems; 2024 WHIMC middle-school camp interview corpus
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: SRL data available by request through DataShop (project IDs 5371 and 5820); WHIMC interview data restricted; codebook artifacts shared through view-only OSF project
evidence_records.Number of documents: 955 utterances in Study 1; 144 interview transcripts in Study 2
evidence_records.Number of participants: 15 students in Study 1; 14 middle-school students in Study 2
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 955 segmented utterances; 144 interview transcripts from a five-day, 15-hour camp
evidence_records.Document length: Study 1 sessions lasted 45–60 minutes with up to 20 minutes of think-aloud; Study 2 transcript lengths not reported
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: human-student educational data, including minors in Study 2; parental consent and participant assent are reported for the camp
evidence_records.Exact model/version: gpt-4o-2024-08-06 in Study 1; gpt-4o-2024-11-20 in Study 2; temperature 0
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Theory- and data-grounded prompts; Study 2 compares no theory, theory named, full bibliographic references, and full theory papers, with three generations per condition.
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single LLM with repeated independent generations
evidence_records.Agent roles: construct/codebook generator, definition/example proposer, and theory operationalizer
evidence_records.Human role: Researchers selected theories/data, designed prompts, consolidated generations, removed/revised constructs, and evaluated codebooks; the final codebooks are human-refined rather than autonomous model outputs.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: utterance or interview transcript as evidence for theory-linked constructs; generated construct/codebook entry as evaluation object
evidence_records.Generated outputs: construct lists, definitions, inclusion/exclusion guidance, examples, and condition-specific codebooks
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Codebook constructs include examples and are grounded in supplied corpora/theory; an OSF artifact package is linked, though the full generation-to-source lineage and every refinement decision are not machine-auditable.
evidence_records.Baselines: four prompting conditions and human refinement; no independently built human-only codebook evaluated under the same seven-dimension rubric
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: three runs per Study 2 condition (12 codebooks); temperature 0; Study 1 run accounting is not fully enumerated
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: descriptive construct counts only
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Five author evaluators scored consolidated Study 2 codebooks on usefulness, clarity, examples, concreteness, exhaustiveness, complementarity, and theoretical alignment.
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: five coauthor learning-sciences researchers; first two authors also consolidated/refined outputs
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not reported for the seven-dimension ratings
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive mean ratings; no inferential tests or uncertainty estimates
evidence_records.Principal results: Study 1 produced an 11-construct human-refined SRL codebook without adding constructs beyond the model proposals. In Study 2, merely naming the theory scored highest on six of seven practical criteria, while supplying full papers scored highest on theoretical alignment (4.60 versus 3.60 for theory named) but lower on applicability; condition differences were not inferentially tested.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: no measured time, token, energy, or monetary cost
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Parental consent and participant assent are reported for the minor camp participants; direct identifiers are not described in prompts. Broader training-data and hallucination risks are discussed.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: OSF artifact project https://osf.io/g3z4x/?view_only=1effdfc734c64f0db13bd59aed931ae6; model snapshots, temperature, conditions, and several data-access identifiers are reported.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Theories and datasets differ structurally; model pretraining may distort theory; general-purpose GPT-4o may not transfer; codebooks still need question-specific refinement and later coding validation.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Evaluators are unblinded coauthors, the evaluated objects were human-consolidated, no human-only baseline or formal IRR exists, and seven ordinal ratings are reported without uncertainty. “Naming theory” may benefit from model training-data familiarity and cannot isolate theory knowledge from leakage.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Builds on Zambrano et al. automated-coding/code-refinement work, Barany et al. 2024 codebook development, and prior SRL data analyses; dependence should be acknowledged when counting distinct datasets.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Directly motivates controlled context ablations, exact model/version logging, blinded external evaluation, a human-only codebook baseline, and immutable provenance from source excerpts through generated and human-refined codebooks.
