evidence_records.Title: Emergent Convergence in Multi-Agent LLM Annotation
evidence_records.Authors: Angelina Parfenova; Alexander Denzler; Juergen Pfeffer
evidence_records.Peer-reviewed status: peer reviewed workshop paper in ACL Anthology proceedings
evidence_records.Publication history notes: Archival ACL Anthology version; a matching arXiv record is part of the same publication family.
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official ACL Anthology PDF inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: ACL/arXiv publication family; one retained report
evidence_records.Research objective: Characterize how discussion among heterogeneous LLM annotators changes code convergence, semantic diversity, influence, confidence, and representational structure.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: multi-agent qualitative annotation/coding experiment
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Five LLMs independently produced short qualitative codes for 500 high-disagreement toxicity comments, then saw accumulated summaries of other agents’ prior outputs over 1–5 fixed-order rounds in 2-, 3-, and 5-model configurations and five prompt variants.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: inductive short-code generation conditioned on evolving peer outputs
evidence_records.Dataset name: Jigsaw Unintended Bias in Toxicity Classification high-disagreement subset
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: public benchmark dataset; exact 500-item sample and complete outputs were not located in a repository
evidence_records.Number of participants: not applicable; public online comments with original annotator labels
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 7,500 multi-agent discussions and approximately 125,000 generated utterances across configurations
evidence_records.Document length: comments were sampled with a minimum length of 100 words; full distribution not reported
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: public toxicity comments may contain harmful or identity-related content; the paper treats them as public benchmark data
evidence_records.Model family: Meta Llama, DeepSeek, Google Gemma, and Mistral
evidence_records.Exact model/version: Llama 4 Maverick; Llama 3.3 70B; DeepSeek-R1 70B; Gemma and Mistral variants named without fully reproducible checkpoints/configuration in the inspected text
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: five coding prompts; agents receive accumulated summaries of other models’ preceding outputs between fixed-order rounds
evidence_records.Agent roles: peer qualitative coders whose prior-round summaries become context for subsequent coding
evidence_records.Human role: Researchers selected the dataset/configurations/prompts and interpreted convergence; no human qualitative expert judged code quality or meaning preservation.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: comment-level generated code and model-round trajectory
evidence_records.Generated outputs: short qualitative codes, round summaries, confidence language, convergence trajectories, and representation diagnostics
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Outputs remain associated with comment/configuration/round in the experimental analysis, but no public machine-readable lineage package for the 125,000 utterances was verified.
evidence_records.Baselines: round-1 independent outputs, different group sizes, round depths, prompts, and model mixtures; no human-code or oracle-quality baseline
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: 500 discussions per configuration, 7,500 discussions overall; generation seeds and repeat replications of identical configurations are not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: ROUGE-1/2/L, sentence-embedding cosine similarity, UMAP, TwoNN intrinsic dimensionality, TF-IDF self-consistency, lexical confidence, toxicity, and 190 ELFEN linguistic features
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: none
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: none for code validity or interpretive quality
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not applicable; model-model similarity is not human inter-rater reliability
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive trajectory and configuration comparisons; inferential uncertainty across comments/configurations is limited
evidence_records.Principal results: Model outputs generally converge lexically and semantically while intrinsic dimensionality contracts. Peak final-round ROUGE-L reached 0.807 in a three-model/four-round Prompt-1 setting; intrinsic dimensionality dropped sharply in several group sizes. Influence shifted across models over rounds. The same convergence may represent semantic flattening rather than better codes.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: no monetary, latency, energy, or human-time evaluation
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Authors note use of an existing public dataset, no new human-subject collection, and risks from biased/toxic content; no detailed treatment of original commenters’ consent or downstream representational harm.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: ACL paper and mathematical/experimental descriptions are public; no verified code/output repository and several exact model serving details are missing.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Convergence is not necessarily truth or quality; models may reinforce bias, collapse diversity, and depend on prompt/model composition.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: All headline evidence is model-output similarity without human semantic adjudication; ROUGE and embedding compression reward homogenization. Fixed interaction order, accumulated summaries, incomplete checkpoint details, and no replicated seeds confound social influence with context accumulation.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Distinct multi-agent annotation study; matching preprint/ACL records should count once.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Strong warning that agent agreement is not validity. ARR evaluation should pair convergence with blinded human quality, minority/edge-case retention, source grounding, order randomization, and stability across seeds.

evidence_records.Full citation: Zhang, He, Chuhao Wu, Jingyi Xie, Fiona Rubino, Sydney Graver, Jie Cai, ChanMin Kim, and John M. Carroll. 2025. Exploring Inductive and Deductive Qualitative Coding with AI: Investigating Inter-Rater Reliability between Large Language Model and Human Coders. Human-Computer Interaction & Emerging Technologies 195: 142–152. https://doi.org/10.54941/ahfe1006232.
evidence_records.Title: Exploring Inductive and Deductive Qualitative Coding with AI: Investigating Inter-Rater Reliability between Large Language Model and Human Coders
evidence_records.Authors: He Zhang; Chuhao Wu; Jingyi Xie; Fiona Rubino; Sydney Graver; Jie Cai; ChanMin Kim; John M. Carroll
evidence_records.Venue: Human-Computer Interaction & Emerging Technologies, AHFE 2025, volume 195, pages 142–152
evidence_records.Publication history notes: Official AHFE Open Access proceedings version inspected.
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official proceedings PDF inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: QualiGPT tool paper; distinct from later/related Penn State qualitative-analysis workflow papers but shares authors/tool lineage
evidence_records.Research objective: Evaluate LLM support for inductive and deductive qualitative coding and introduce the QualiGPT API workflow.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: inductive and deductive qualitative coding with human–LLM intercoder-reliability comparison
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: From 1,000 public TwitchDev Discord posts, topic modeling selected two topics and 200 posts for two-RA open coding. Researchers consolidated 171 labels into a 54-label codebook, then two RAs and three independent GPT-4 runs coded another 200 posts; GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 were also tested.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: both: inductive open labeling followed by deductive multi-label codebook application
evidence_records.Dataset name: 1,000 TwitchDev public Discord posts
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: source messages described as public; the analyzed dataset itself was not verified as released
evidence_records.Number of documents: 1,000 total posts; 200 inductive and a separate 200 deductive evaluation entries
evidence_records.Number of participants: unknown number of Discord users; two research assistants plus one senior researcher for human codebook work
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 1,000 posts; 400 sampled evaluation entries
evidence_records.Document length: single Discord entries; distribution not reported
evidence_records.Language: English is implied by prompts/examples but not explicitly stated
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: public community messages; authors say sensitive user data were excluded, but operational criteria and consent/ethics review are not reported
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5; exact snapshots not reported; default temperature 0.7
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: role/task/background/data-format/output-format template; inductive prompts requested one code per entry and deductive prompts supplied the 54-label codebook; malformed outputs could be regenerated
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single model per run; model outputs are compared as coders
evidence_records.Agent roles: open-code generator and deductive multi-label coder
evidence_records.Human role: Two RAs independently open-coded, consolidated/refined a codebook with a senior researcher, deductively coded the evaluation set, selected prompt regenerations, and remained final validators.
evidence_records.Generated outputs: open labels/themes, deductive multi-label assignments, codebook-support artifacts, and QualiGPT tables
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: QualiGPT stores original text beside assigned codes and indices; the paper does not provide a public immutable dataset/output package or a full trail of regenerated responses.
evidence_records.Baselines: two human RAs, GPT-4 repeated three times, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5; no expert gold adjudication or held-out codebook-development split
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: three independent GPT-4 deductive runs; one reported run each for GPT-4o and Claude 3.5; seeds not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Cohen’s kappa for inductive human–GPT mapping; Fleiss’ kappa for deductive coder sets
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Human labels and codebook serve as comparison; no blinded expert quality rating of model-discovered themes
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two research assistants and one senior researcher; domain/qualitative expertise not fully characterized
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: Inductive human–GPT Cohen’s κ=.57; deductive human-human κ=.73; RA1+RA2+GPT-4 Fleiss κ=.44–.50 (mean .46); GPT-4 self-agreement κ=.87; RA1+RA2+GPT-4o κ=.38; RA1+RA2+Claude 3.5 κ=.42.
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive kappa comparisons; no confidence intervals, significance tests, or prevalence-adjusted sensitivity analysis
evidence_records.Principal results: GPT-4 showed moderate agreement with human open coding and lower agreement with humans than the two RAs achieved with each other in deductive coding. GPT-4 was internally consistent, but newer GPT-4o/Claude comparisons were lower. These results support assistance, not the article’s stronger implication of maintained contextual depth or standardized validity.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: Manual coding is described as hours/week, but no controlled time, latency, token, or monetary comparison is reported
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: QualiGPT is framed as addressing privacy and sensitive user data were excluded; no IRB/consent decision, deidentification protocol, or platform-terms analysis is reported.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: QualiGPT repository: https://github.com/KindOPSTAR/QualiGPT; exact data, model snapshots, complete prompts/outputs, and regeneration log were not verified as available.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Prompt engineering, domain-specific training, fabricated content, model evolution, and need for human oversight.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Open-code mapping for κ is underexplained; multi-label Fleiss κ assumptions are unclear; codebook creation and evaluation are not cleanly independent; temp=.7 plus output regeneration creates selection risk; no qualitative expert gold standard or confidence intervals.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Shares QualiGPT/Penn State author and tool lineage; treat datasets/contributions separately but avoid calling each paper an independent system family.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Motivates exact multi-label metric definitions, adjudicated mappings, fixed regeneration rules, prompt/model snapshots, split development/evaluation data, external experts, and confidence intervals rather than a single κ headline.

evidence_records.Full citation: Nguyen-Trung, Kien, and Ngoc Lan Nguyen. 2026. Narrative-Integrated Thematic Analysis (NITA): How Can LLMs Support Theme Generation Without Coding? Qualitative Research in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/14780887.2026.2638348. (2025 SSRN preprint: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5163884.)
evidence_records.Title: Narrative-Integrated Thematic Analysis (NITA): How Can LLMs Support Theme Generation Without Coding?
evidence_records.Authors: Kien Nguyen-Trung; Ngoc Lan Nguyen
evidence_records.Venue: Qualitative Research in Psychology, online first
evidence_records.Publication type: peer-reviewed journal article; publication family originated as a 2025 SSRN preprint
evidence_records.Publication history notes: The screened 2025 record was SSRN DOI 10.2139/ssrn.5163884. It was superseded by the peer-reviewed open-access article published online 2026-03-06, DOI 10.1080/14780887.2026.2638348; extracted once as one publication family.
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; publisher full article/PDF text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: 2025 SSRN preprint to 2026 journal VOR; extends Nguyen-Trung 2025 GAITA using the same Down East dataset and analytic question but a noncoding workflow and the full corpus
evidence_records.Research objective: Develop and illustrate NITA, a pragmatist, reflexive, human-led approach in which an LLM supports thematic analysis without segment-level coding.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: nonpositivist, noncoding thematic analysis integrating narrative, matrix, Framework Analysis, Iterative Thematic Inquiry, and the PERFECT reflexive procedure
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Two researchers familiarized themselves with 11 public interviews, configured a custom ChatGPT GPT with ROLE/GUIDES instructions and uploaded transcripts, generated candidate themes repeatedly, built participant narratives, compared gender groups, cross-checked quotations, debated/revised themes, and authored a six-stage meta-narrative.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: abductive/hybrid; iterative movement between prior beliefs, candidate themes, individual cases, group comparisons, and revised explanations
evidence_records.Domain: qualitative methodology / environmental and rural-community perceptions
evidence_records.Dataset name: Environmental Change in Down East sample project
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: public secondary sample data used with Lumivero permission
evidence_records.Number of participants: 11 interviewees from Carteret County, North Carolina
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 20,832 words in the current article (one manuscript passage reports 20,420; this internal discrepancy should be preserved)
evidence_records.Document length: approximately six pages or about 2,000 words per interview
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: secondary public interview data; original interviews concern community, livelihoods, identity, and environmental change
evidence_records.Exact model/version: GPT-4o through a custom ChatGPT “My GPTs” instance; exact snapshot, temperature, seed, and retrieval settings not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: ROLE and GUIDES system customization; PERFECT planning/reflexive log; stage-specific prompts for three-or-more candidate-theme runs, individual narratives and uncaptured themes, cross-gender matrices, theme naming, meta-narrative, and Mermaid map.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: No weight tuning; custom GPT instructions and retrieval-augmented generation over 11 uploaded PDFs
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single customized LLM used by two human researchers
evidence_records.Agent roles: candidate-theme suggester, narrative/matrix generator, quotation retriever, uncaptured-theme prompter, comparison assistant, and diagram-syntax generator
evidence_records.Human role: Both researchers read the data, designed and updated PERFECT, checked quotations against transcripts, interpreted outputs through their positionalities, decided theme inclusion/naming/relationships, and retained analytic and representational authority.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: whole interview and individual/cross-case narrative rather than segmented coded unit
evidence_records.Generated outputs: candidate themes, participant-level narrative matrices with quotations, possible missing themes, gender comparison tables, six final themes, a meta-narrative, and Mermaid syntax
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Prompts/results are reproduced selectively and PERFECT is proposed as audit trail/reflexive diary; researchers explicitly cross-check source quotations, but no complete export of chats, retrieval hits, source spans, and human edits was verified.
evidence_records.Baselines: qualitative comparison with Nguyen-Trung 2025 GAITA on Section Q1 of the same 11 interviews; no independent human-only reanalysis of the full 20,832-word corpus
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: candidate-theme prompt run at least three times; other prompts iterated, but full run counts and seeds are not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: none
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Two author-researchers reflexively compare, cross-check, discuss, revise, and compare themes with the earlier GAITA theme list; no blinded external evaluators
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: two qualitative researchers, one with prior experience analyzing this same dataset and the other initially new to it
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not calculated; interpretive disagreement and positionality are discussed rather than reduced to reliability
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: none
evidence_records.Principal results: Five themes broadly resembled the earlier coding-based GAITA analysis; GPT-4o repeatedly proposed a sixth “resistance to change/development” theme. The researchers initially disagreed, used positionality and case-level evidence to retain and refine it as “We don’t like unsustainable change,” then linked six themes in a human-authored meta-narrative. This is a worked methodological illustration, not an independent accuracy validation.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: no measured time, cognitive workload, API cost, tokens, or energy; no coding step is performed
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Uses secondary data with permission and explicitly discusses data rights, privacy/consent, bias, interpretive sufficiency, agency, IRB disclosure, local/secure tools, audit trails, and representational responsibility.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Key prompts, tables, screenshots, and workflow are in the open article; the public sample dataset is identified. Custom GPT/chat histories, complete PERFECT sheet, exact snapshot/settings, and machine-readable outputs are not verified as released.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: NITA is not congruent with every epistemology or researcher, AI safeguards/law evolve, and researchers must retain intellectual leadership; the article offers a worked example rather than broad validation.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: One author previously analyzed the same data, comparison reuses the same corpus/question, no independent human-only full-corpus baseline exists, and theme similarity is judged qualitatively. Internal corpus-size inconsistency (20,420 vs 20,832), opaque custom-GPT retrieval, and no stability quantification constrain reproducibility.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Direct dependency on Nguyen-Trung 2025 GAITA and the same Lumivero/Duke Down East interviews; the 2025 SSRN and 2026 journal article are one report family.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: NITA materially strengthens the human-authority and reflexive-ledger design case, while exposing the need for versioned full chat/RAG provenance, independent assessors, blind comparisons, run stability, and explicit dependency-family reporting.

evidence_records.Full citation: Wiebe, Joel P., Rubaina Khan, Samantha Burns, and James D. Slotta. 2025. Qualitative Research in the Age of LLMs: A Human-in-the-Loop Approach to Hybrid Thematic Analysis. Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences (ICLS 2025), 1123–1131. https://doi.org/10.22318/icls2025.322165.
evidence_records.Title: Qualitative Research in the Age of LLMs: A Human-in-the-Loop Approach to Hybrid Thematic Analysis
evidence_records.Authors: Joel P. Wiebe; Rubaina Khan; Samantha Burns; James D. Slotta
evidence_records.Venue: Proceedings of the 19th International Conference of the Learning Sciences (ICLS 2025), pages 1123–1131
evidence_records.Publication history notes: Official ISLS repository proceedings version inspected.
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; official ISLS full text inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: HHitL-TA framework/tool demonstration; no duplicate publication family verified
evidence_records.Research objective: Introduce a six-stage Hybrid Human-in-the-Loop Thematic Analysis framework and tool, then illustrate it on engineering-student motivation reflections grounded in Social Cognitive Career Theory.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: hybrid deductive–inductive human-in-the-loop thematic analysis grounded primarily in reflexive thematic analysis
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: A primary researcher established SCCT constructs, compared human/LLM coding on 39 documents, iteratively accepted/merged/rejected LLM codes on 40 documents, used Gemini 1.5 Pro to code 175 reflections and generate themes/magnitude scores/summaries, then humans reviewed, revised, triangulated with latent classes, and retained final synthesis.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: hybrid: deductive SCCT dimensions with inductive codes/themes and human refinement
evidence_records.Dataset name: undergraduate engineering-design motivation reflections linked to SCCT latent-class profiles
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: restricted student data; anonymized before model use; no dataset release
evidence_records.Number of documents: 196 candidate reflections; 175 with latent-class membership probability above 90% analyzed; 39 in construct check and 40 in initial-code sample
evidence_records.Number of participants: not explicitly separated from document count; 175 included student reflections
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: nearly 1,000 reflections existed in the broader project; 175 at the initial time point were analyzed; 2,622 extracts were coded
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: human-student reflections; records were anonymized and stored per participant before model use
evidence_records.Exact model/version: Gemini 1.5 Pro via Vertex AI; exact checkpoint, temperature, seed, and safety settings not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Stage-specific templates combining persona, data payload, research question, SCCT construct codebook, existing codes/themes, task instructions, and JSON schemas; full prompts are not reproduced in the paper.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: none; progressive prompt priming and structured JSON/tool workflow
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single LLM in a staged workflow
evidence_records.Agent roles: construct coder, inductive-code generator, full-corpus coder, emergent-code proposer, merge recommender, theme/magnitude/summary generator, and visualization-data producer
evidence_records.Human role: Humans define theory/questions, familiarize with data, approve/reject/merge codes, revise instructions, review theme structures and magnitude/summaries, investigate discrepancies, author synthesis, and retain final interpretive control.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: student reflection, source extract, code, theme, participant/class profile
evidence_records.Generated outputs: source-linked codes and justifications, confidence values, a 435-code refined codebook, 2,622 coded extracts, themes/maps, 1–7 magnitude scores, class summaries, and cross-case displays
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Structured outputs retain excerpts/participant IDs and intermediate artifacts for human review; however, the paper does not release the complete run logs, prompts, human edits, or coded corpus.
evidence_records.Baselines: human–LLM construct coding on a 20% sample; latent-class analysis used for triangulation; no independent human thematic analysis of the full corpus
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: iterative widening on samples and a verification run are described; complete run/seed accounting is not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: Cohen’s kappa for nine constructs; code frequency/diversity/magnitude and latent-class probabilities
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Primary researcher reviews all key staged products; human and LLM independently code 39 documents for construct presence; no blinded external theme-quality panel
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: primary researcher plus plural researchers at later review/synthesis stages; exact number, expertise, and workload by stage are not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: Cohen’s κ > .70 for each of the nine retained constructs on 39 documents; exact construct-level values are not provided
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive code metrics and latent-class probabilities; no inferential validation of model-generated themes or magnitude scores
evidence_records.Principal results: Two of 11 initial SCCT factors were dropped after human/LLM sample coding. On 40 reflections, human review merged 8 and rejected 68 generated codes, then accepted 31 new verification codes, yielding 202 initial codes. Full-corpus generation produced 308 proposed new codes, 31 accepted merges, a final 435-code set, and 2,622 extracts. The Class-A illustration shows how LLM-supported TA surfaced brief prior-experience/social-influence evidence that LCA deemphasized, but the final full five-profile report was still being authored.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: Scalability and efficiency are design motivations; no controlled human-time, API-cost, token, or energy measures
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Anonymization/confidentiality, human control, bias, privacy, IP, passive-researcher risk, and transparent reporting are discussed; formal IRB/consent status is not reported in the paper.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Tool repository: https://github.com/encorelab/ai-theme-analyser. The data, exact prompts/settings, run logs, final codebook, and evaluation outputs were not verified as public.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Need for full-dataset human verification at scale, ongoing risk of LLM error/context loss, and need for stronger reporting guidance and tool refinement.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: The paper claims reflexive TA while operationalizing a large theory-bound codebook, IRR, prevalence metrics, latent classes, and 1–7 magnitude scores. Most model-produced codes/themes lack an independent full-corpus human baseline; model snapshot/settings, reviewer counts, and revision totals are incomplete; the final analysis is unfinished.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Draws on SCCT/LCA work and Bano/related LLM-QDA frameworks but presents a distinct tool/framework and dataset.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Valuable staged human-control architecture and source-extract structure, but ARR should pre-register methodology claims, capture every accept/reject/edit, validate magnitude/theme outputs independently, and separate RTA-compatible reflexivity from coding-reliability metrics.

evidence_records.Full citation: Zhou, Tingting, Mengyao Xing, Yue Hu, Jun Liang, Qi Ren, Yeqin Yang, and Lei Ye. 2025. The Application of Large Language Models in Qualitative Nursing Research: A Scoping Review. Nursing Outlook 73(6): 102544. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.outlook.2025.102544.
evidence_records.Title: The Application of Large Language Models in Qualitative Nursing Research: A Scoping Review
evidence_records.Authors: Tingting Zhou; Mengyao Xing; Yue Hu; Jun Liang; Qi Ren; Yeqin Yang; Lei Ye
evidence_records.Publication history notes: November–December 2025 issue; publisher full HTML inspected.
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; publisher full HTML inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: secondary scoping review of 11 studies; constituent primary studies overlap the evidence base and must not be counted as independent new evaluations
evidence_records.Research objective: Map LLM application scenarios, effects, evaluation methods, and challenges in qualitative nursing research.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: JBI-method scoping review reported with PRISMA-ScR
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Authors searched 11 databases through April 2025, deduplicated 2,478 hits to 1,883, screened titles/abstracts and 37 full texts, and retained 11 studies; they descriptively synthesized task, effect, assessment, and challenge categories.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: secondary evidence mapping; not a primary coding system
evidence_records.Dataset name: 11-study qualitative-nursing/LLM scoping-review corpus
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: published literature; protocol in Appendix S1; complete extraction data availability not verified
evidence_records.Number of documents: 2,478 identified; 1,883 after duplicates; 37 full texts considered; 11 included studies
evidence_records.Number of participants: not applicable at review level; constituent-study participant counts vary
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 11 databases searched through April 2025
evidence_records.Language: language restrictions/translation procedure not fully visible in the inspected text
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: no new participant data; constituent studies may involve sensitive nursing/health narratives
evidence_records.Exact model/version: heterogeneous and incompletely reported across included studies
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: heterogeneous across constituent studies; review does not operationalize its own LLM workflow
evidence_records.Agent roles: across studies: topic/theme generation, role-playing, interview-question generation, text analysis, and codebook work
evidence_records.Human role: Reviewers screened/extracted/synthesized; human roles in primary studies vary and are summarized at aggregate level.
evidence_records.Generated outputs: evidence map of scenarios, effects, assessments, and challenges
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: PRISMA-ScR flow and study tables link findings to included studies, but the review-level aggregate cannot replace primary-study methods/results inspection.
evidence_records.Baselines: not applicable at review level; included studies use heterogeneous human comparisons
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: not applicable
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: descriptive review counts; constituent metrics include human-output similarity and efficiency
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: review screening/extraction; reviewer count and independent duplicate procedures require caution if not explicit in full tables/protocol
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: seven-author review team; exact duplicate-screening/extraction assignments not fully reported in the accessible text
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not reported for review screening/extraction in the inspected sections
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive scoping synthesis only
evidence_records.Principal results: Eleven studies were retained from 2,478 records. LLMs were used for topic generation, role play, interview-question generation, and qualitative text analysis; outputs showed moderate-to-high thematic similarity and efficiency, but weaker theoretical-framework application, interview-question generation, and codebook development. The evidence was judged early-stage and heterogeneous.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: Review reports efficiency advantages in constituent studies but does not provide a standardized pooled effect or cost analysis
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: No new participant collection; review discusses privacy, bias, technical constraints, and responsible nursing-research use; protocol and conflict/funding statements are reported.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Appendix S1 protocol and publisher study tables; no verified review repository with full searches, deduplication file, decisions, and extraction forms
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Small, immature, heterogeneous literature; limited analysis depth, simulation accuracy, technical constraints, and evaluation tools
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Only 11 studies and nursing-specific eligibility limit generalization; synthesis phrases such as “moderate-to-high similarity” combine non-equivalent tasks/metrics. Review findings should not be double-counted alongside the same primary studies.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Secondary synthesis whose 11 constituent studies overlap several primary papers in this review.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Useful adjacent map of nursing-specific tasks and gaps; reinforces standardized evaluation and theory-sensitive testing but should not alter ARR rankings as an independent system evaluation.

evidence_records.Full citation: Than, Nga, Leanne Fan, Tina Law, Laura K. Nelson, and Leslie McCall. 2025. Updating “The Future of Coding”: Qualitative Coding with Generative Large Language Models. Sociological Methods & Research, online first. https://doi.org/10.1177/00491241251339188.
evidence_records.Title: Updating “The Future of Coding”: Qualitative Coding with Generative Large Language Models
evidence_records.Authors: Nga Than; Leanne Fan; Tina Law; Laura K. Nelson; Leslie McCall
evidence_records.Venue: Sociological Methods & Research, online first, pages 1–40
evidence_records.Publication history notes: 2025 Sage journal version of record; author-hosted VOR inspected.
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; author-hosted VOR inspected 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: extends McCall 2013 human coding and Nelson et al. 2018 computational replication on the same newsweekly corpus; current LLM study is not an independent dataset
evidence_records.Research objective: Test whether open and proprietary generative LLMs can reproduce two qualitative news-article classifications and derive a prompt/model comparison workflow for qualitative coders.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: iterative qualitative coding/classification with natural-language LLM prompts and interprompt/intermodel validation
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Models classify 1,253 long newsweekly articles as relevant/irrelevant and 786 relevant articles for inequality, using zero-shot no-definition, researcher-definition, LLM-definition, and two-example few-shot prompts; predictions are scored against prior human labels and compared across prompts/models.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: predominantly deductive classification from an established codebook, with iterative/LLM-generated definition construction
evidence_records.Domain: sociology / historical news media / economic inequality
evidence_records.Dataset name: McCall/Nelson U.S. newsweekly inequality corpus
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: article full texts are copyrighted; metadata, generated outputs, and replication/reproduction materials are on GitHub
evidence_records.Number of documents: 1,253 articles for relevance; 786 relevant articles for inequality/few-shot tasks
evidence_records.Number of participants: not applicable; more than six human research assistants created the original labels
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 1,253 Time, Newsweek, and U.S. News & World Report articles from 1980–2012
evidence_records.Document length: long-form articles; mean length is discussed, but the exact value was not extracted; texts were truncated when exceeding model windows
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: copyrighted news text; no human-subject data
evidence_records.Model family: Meta Llama, Google Gemma, and OpenAI GPT
evidence_records.Exact model/version: Ollama-hosted prequantized Llama3 70B, Llama3.1 70B, Gemma2 27B, and proprietary GPT-4; exact GPT snapshot and some quantization tags are not clearly reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: two-step binary schema; system/meta statements; zero-shot no definition, hand-condensed codebook definition, model-generated 7–10-bullet definition with human merge/deduplication, and two randomly selected examples for few-shot; output requires label plus one-sentence rationale
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: Main analyses use no tuning; supplementary Gemma2 and BERT fine-tuning tests use up to 1,000 labeled documents
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single model per classification; ensembles/majority votes are computed post hoc across prompts or models
evidence_records.Agent roles: binary document classifier, definition summarizer, and one-sentence rationale generator
evidence_records.Human role: Researchers built/condensed definitions, chose prompt structure/sequencing/examples, manually merged LLM definitions, interpreted natural-language outputs, and retained validation responsibility.
evidence_records.Generated outputs: binary labels, one-sentence justifications, model-generated definitions, agreement matrices, and majority-vote labels
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Outputs and replication code are public and rationales refer to document content; copyrighted texts are not released, and sentence rationales are not equivalent to verified source-span provenance.
evidence_records.Baselines: original human coding, prior supervised ML median F1s, four LLMs, definition/prompt variants, and majority votes
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: temperature 0 and a seed set; one reported execution per model/prompt task plus prompt/model ensembles; full repeated identical-run stability is not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: weighted precision, recall, F1; interprompt/intermodel Fleiss’ kappa; majority-vote F1; supplemental fine-tuning curves
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Predictions are scored against preexisting human labels from an original multi-RA project; no new blinded qualitative judgment of rationales or emergent insights
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: original project used more than six undergraduate/graduate RAs; current authors include researchers from the original and replication studies
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: Interprompt/intermodel Fleiss κ=.62–.88; original human-label reliability is discussed via prior publications rather than re-reported as a single comparable estimate
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: weighted F1 comparisons and descriptive agreement; no confidence intervals or paired significance testing reported for most model differences
evidence_records.Principal results: Zero-shot weighted F1 ranged .74–.83 for relevance and .70–.74 for inequality; few-shot F1 ranged .60–.75 and harmed some open models. Researcher definitions did not consistently beat no definition; LLM definitions marginally helped some models/tasks. GPT-4 was usually only .01–.03 above the best open model except few-shot. Majority voting raised the worst F1 from .59 to .75 but the best only from .83 to .84; full agreement covered 74%–91% of documents. Agreement can reflect shared bias, not validity.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: Each GPT-4 test cost approximately US$50–$70; open models avoid API charges but require hardware/electricity. No human-time experiment; authors state agreement triage may redirect rather than necessarily reduce human coding.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Discusses proprietary model, environmental, bias, reproducibility, copyright, training-data contamination, and open-source tradeoffs; no human subjects.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: https://github.com/lknelson/future-of-coding-revisited contains metadata, generated outputs, and replication/reproduction materials; supplemental appendices are online. Copyright prevents full-text redistribution.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: Long/noisy English news familiar to model training; possible corpus contamination; truncation/context limits; prompt sensitivity; incomplete fine-tuning; transfer to unfamiliar domains uncertain.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: This is supervised binary classification, not open-ended thematic interpretation; same corpus underlies the human and prior-ML baselines. Model snapshots/quantization details and repeated-run stability are incomplete; random few-shot examples are not replicated; most differences lack uncertainty.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Direct longitudinal dependency on McCall 2013 and Nelson et al. 2018; those papers and this article form one dataset/evaluation family.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Major evidence for open-vs-proprietary comparison, prompt/model ensembles, and cost reporting; ARR should add exact checkpoints, repeated samples, confidence intervals, provenance, and a separate open-ended interpretation benchmark.

evidence_records.Full citation: Gustavsen, David, Holly M. Surbaugh, and Mark Emmons. 2025. Using Generative AI for Qualitative Coding. Library Trends 73(3): 213–242. https://doi.org/10.1353/lib.2025.a961193.
evidence_records.Title: Using Generative AI for Qualitative Coding
evidence_records.Authors: David Gustavsen; Holly M. Surbaugh; Mark Emmons
evidence_records.Publication history notes: February 2025 issue; Project MUSE version of record, CC BY 4.0.
evidence_records.Citation count, source, and retrieval da: not collected; complete VOR text inspected through the publisher-rendered/CC BY full-text copy 2026-08-24
evidence_records.Relationship/dependence family: Reanalysis of the authors’ 2021–2024 graduate-student library study (Surbaugh et al. 2024); same interviews/human themes, distinct AI comparison report
evidence_records.Research objective: Compare ChatGPT-4 first- and second-level qualitative coding with a prior human team’s analysis and assess credible roles for the model in academic-library research.
evidence_records.Claimed qualitative methodology: descriptive/in-vivo first-level coding followed by second-level pattern coding and thematic comparison
evidence_records.Actual operationalized methodology: Human baseline: five librarians coded 20 deidentified interviews over about 16 months, producing 898 codes, 19 categories, and five themes. AI study removed one reidentification-risk transcript; two researchers independently prompted ChatGPT-4 on 19 transcripts, combined 1,287 generated codes, ran two second-level procedures, and the three authors qualitatively scored theme/subtheme similarity.
evidence_records.Inductive, deductive, or hybrid: inductive open/in-vivo and pattern coding, with prompt revisions informed by the human process but without giving ChatGPT the final human themes
evidence_records.Dataset name: University of New Mexico graduate-student critical-incident interview corpus
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: restricted institutional interview data; not released
evidence_records.Number of documents: 20 original transcripts; 19 sent to ChatGPT after one high-reidentification-risk transcript was excluded
evidence_records.Number of participants: 20 graduate students originally; 19 in the AI analysis
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 19 deidentified semistructured interview transcripts; ChatGPT generated 1,287 first-level codes (568 and 719 from two workflows)
evidence_records.Document length: second workflow split transcripts into 2,000–4,000-word segments; total words not reported
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: institutional human-subject interviews containing intersecting identities, programs, research topics, unionization, finances, and other potentially identifying context
evidence_records.Exact model/version: ChatGPT 4; ChatGPT 4o appeared only as the study ended and was not evaluated; exact snapshot/settings not reported
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: Two parallel workflows: whole-transcript qualitative-researcher persona with iterative requests for more codes, and a custom academic-librarian GPT over 2,000–4,000-word chunks with a formatting example; second-level prompts grouped all 1,287 codes or batches of 100, then requested categories, themes, subthemes, inference, and relationships.
evidence_records.Fine-tuning or adaptation: No weight tuning; one custom GPT configured with instructions/example spreadsheet
evidence_records.Single-agent or multi-agent: single chatbot used through two human-operated workflows
evidence_records.Agent roles: descriptive/in-vivo coder, pattern coder, category/theme generator, inference prompter, quote retriever, and failed graphic generator
evidence_records.Human role: Humans deidentified data twice, removed a risky transcript, engineered/repeated prompts, combined outputs, selected the richer AI theme set, compared it with the prior analysis, interpreted discrepancies, and retained primary second-level judgment.
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: meaningful sentence/paragraph segment, first-level code, category/subtheme, and theme
evidence_records.Generated outputs: 1,287 first-level codes with quotations, categories/subthemes, five final themes, similarity table, and attempted thematic chart
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: Generated codes were paired with quotes and transcripts were known to evaluators; however, ChatGPT sometimes lost structure or claimed nonexistent downloads, saturation/completeness was unverifiable, and no durable chat/output package was released.
evidence_records.Baselines: prior five-librarian human analysis; two distinct ChatGPT first-/second-level workflows; no alternative model
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: many iterative prompts per transcript and two main workflows; exact run count, seed, temperature, and rerun stability not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: none; author-created ordinal similarity rubric 0–3 is based on human judgment
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: Three authors compared human theme descriptions with AI subthemes using a 0–3 rubric, checked displaced matches, and catalogued ideas missing on each side; not blinded, and no independent external evaluator
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: three current librarian-researcher authors; two participated in the original human study, while the third was initially shielded from its final findings
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: No coefficient for the current 0–3 comparison; original team used shared coding, pair review, audit, and consensus
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive counts and qualitative comparison; no inferential analysis
evidence_records.Principal results: ChatGPT generated 1,287 first-level codes versus 898 human codes and produced five themes with moderate surface alignment. It was strong on concrete actions but missed/flattened emotion, context, trust, teaching/employee roles, equity/basic-needs issues, and—despite librarian persona and direct questions—the library itself. Two human themes had no AI equivalent; several AI subthemes had no human equivalent. Authors advise first-level assistance only and reject the model as primary second-level analyst.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: ChatGPT first-level workflow took about four hours versus months of human work; an optimized second-level model took under one hour versus just over a year around human work schedules. Authors explicitly state credible collaborative second-level use does not eliminate human time.
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: Original consent allowed reuse but did not explicitly authorize LLM use; the UNM IRB allowed the follow-up. Authors performed a second deidentification pass and excluded one participant at reidentification risk, while critically noting that such exclusion can silence marginalized voices.
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: Full CC BY article includes substantial prompts and appendices, but transcripts, complete chats/outputs, custom GPT configuration, and exact model settings are not public.
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: One higher-education domain likely familiar to ChatGPT; one transcript removed; coding only; prompt dependence; ChatGPT-4 only; other models/tools may differ.
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Evaluators/authors overlap the baseline team; the AI theme set was selected after seeing two workflows; first-level “substantial similarity” is assessed only on a subset without formal scoring; no complete-output audit or run stability; massive time differences exclude prompt development, verification, and the original team’s context-building benefits.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Direct reanalysis/dependency on Surbaugh et al. 2024 and the same UNM corpus; should not count as an independent human dataset family.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Materially strengthens the case for staged task allocation: LLM first-pass coding may save time, but interpretive second-level synthesis needs domain experts. ARR should test contextual/theme omissions, marginalized-voice retention, blinded assessors, complete source lineage, and verification-adjusted time.

evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Strong comparator for rare-code stress tests, selective human adjudication, error taxonomy, and efficiency/reliability trade-offs.

evidence_records.Dataset name: ICMP engineering-design dialogue and GenAI-supported lesson-plan peer-assessment dialogue
evidence_records.Public or restricted data: transcripts not publicly released; example outputs/code are shared
evidence_records.Number of participants: 38 student dyads (76 students)
evidence_records.Approximate corpus size: 214,696 words: 134,256 Task A and 80,440 Task B
evidence_records.Document length: long dialogues segmented for model context limits
evidence_records.Sensitive-data status: classroom student dialogue; data-handling/consent details are limited and authors state ethical clearance was not required
evidence_records.Exact model/version: Llama 3.1, Llama 3.3, Llama 4, Qwen3 for coding; GPT-4o for prompt iteration, synthesis and machine rating
evidence_records.Prompting strategy: self-prompting, chain-of-thought, and in-context zero-shot prompting; temperature .8; multi-turn GPT-4o prompt refinement
evidence_records.Agent roles: open LLMs code group transcripts; GPT-4o synthesizes task-level constructs and rates outputs
evidence_records.Human role: researchers refine prompts, verify synthesized schemes, rate code quality, compare with theory, and interpret limitations
evidence_records.Unit of analysis: segmented peer-dialogue transcript and induced CPS construct
evidence_records.Generated outputs: open codes, synthesized code schemes, five-dimension ratings, and framework-overlap analyses
evidence_records.Evidence/provenance mechanism: example code, three prompt templates, one coding output and one GPT-4o analysis are shared; comprehensive source-to-code trace is not released
evidence_records.Baselines: three prompt strategies; Llama 3.1/3.3/4 versus Qwen3; four established CPS frameworks
evidence_records.Number of runs or seeds: single reported large-scale pass per displayed model/prompt configuration; stochastic replication not reported
evidence_records.Automatic metrics: GPT-4o and human 0–2 ratings for clarity, concreteness, objectivity, granularity and specificity
evidence_records.Human-evaluation design: human experts rate the same synthesized constructs as GPT-4o and verify comparisons with established CPS frameworks
evidence_records.Number and expertise of evaluators: human experts/research authors; exact number and independence not reported
evidence_records.Inter-rater reliability: not reported
evidence_records.Statistical analysis: descriptive mean rubric scores; no inferential tests
evidence_records.Principal results: Outputs showed moderate-to-high human/machine rubric alignment, but LLMs systematically rated clarity/coherence more highly. In-context prompting performed best overall; models showed low recall, instability, overlapping codes and theoretical drift.
evidence_records.Efficiency or cost results: API-based full-corpus coding was feasible; time/cost not quantified
evidence_records.Ethics and privacy treatment: authors state ethical clearance was not required; paper discusses privacy, fairness, teacher agency, and responsible use but gives limited participant-data governance detail
evidence_records.Reproducibility resources: OSF view-only package https://osf.io/sm5zp/ with API code, three templates and selected example outputs; raw corpus and full outputs not verified as available
evidence_records.Author-reported limitations: limited models/tasks, subjectivity in human synthesis, two educational contexts, uncertain transfer, transparency/agency/ethical concerns
evidence_records.Additional validity concerns: Rubric ratings of generated constructs do not measure source coverage or coding recall; GPT-4o both helps generate and evaluates outputs, creating dependence.
evidence_records.Relationship to prior papers: Builds on prompt engineering and open-model inductive coding for learning analytics.
evidence_records.Relevance to the proposed ARR project: Useful open-model prompt baseline and negative result source for judge dependence, recall, theoretical grounding, model instability, and release completeness.

Appropriateness of its dataset.rationale: Partial/claim-limited: 71 academic-identity interview segments; Finance-News600, PubMed-RCT600, ECHR-A, Moral-Stories, WMT20 QE, XNLI-zh; 710 primary segment–code units / 5,680 model decisions; 1,242 audit judgments reported; six external datasets

Availability of data, prompts, code, and.rationale: Adequate for the stated claim: Harvard Dataverse DOI 10.7910/DVN/G1AYGK with prompts, JSON payloads, outputs, scripts, notebooks, figures and anonymized data subset; Claude 3.5 and 3.7 Sonnet; GPT-4o and o3-mini; Gemini 2.5 Flash; DeepSeek V3 and Reasoner; release-date labels in paper are not all conventional snapshot IDs
